EMERGING TECH RESEARCH
Tariffs and Supply Chain 
Challenges in Clean Energy
Tariffs are compounding the existing challenges faced 
by clean energy supply chains
PitchBook is a Morningstar company providing the most comprehensive, most 
accurate, and hard-to-find data for professionals doing business in the private markets.
Key takeaways
•	
Clean energy development and adoption are exposed to significant risk due to 
geographically concentrated supply chains. The falling cost of low-carbon energy 
technologies such as solar, wind, and lithium batteries has accelerated their 
adoption. However, their dependence on critical minerals and components from 
geographically concentrated supply chains—particularly in China and Southeast 
Asia—creates exposure to geopolitical and operational disruptions.
•	
US tariffs are impacting the country’s ability to develop and adopt clean energy 
technologies. Recent tariffs from the US are affecting clean energy supply chains, 
increasing costs, and limiting access to key components for the energy sector. 
The uncertainty for investors and project developers further complicates supply 
chain management and long-term planning across a broad range of technologies, 
including renewables, energy storage, and clean fuel generation.
•	
VC investment in clean energy will be affected by this uncertainty, but there 
are also opportunities for VC-backed companies to develop technologies in 
energy storage, recycling, and mineral extraction. VC investment is fueling 
innovation and development in areas such as lithium battery recycling, direct 
lithium extraction, subsurface resource detection, and nonlithium battery 
chemistries. These emerging technologies have the potential to reduce 
supply chain dependencies, lower environmental impact, and support the 
global clean energy transition.
•	
The geographic concentration of clean energy hardware production, mineral 
extraction, and mineral processing represents a risk for the global clean energy 
transition. Production of clean energy hardware—particularly solar modules, 
batteries, and electrolyzers—is highly concentrated in Asia, and scaling up 
mineral production and manufacturing from low levels in other regions is costly. 
Some critical minerals have very few alternative supply chains due to limited 
viable mineral deposits, and others depend on high-volume processing of other 
minerals because they are produced as byproducts of other mineral extraction/
refining processes.

2
Tariffs and Supply Chain Challenges in Clean Energy
Overview
The clean energy transition continues to accelerate, driven by falling costs for 
low-carbon energy technologies; the continued electrification of transportation, 
manufacturing, and the built environment; higher consumption of energy produced 
by low-carbon technologies; and increased energy demand from growing datacenter 
energy requirements. Low-carbon energy technologies are varied, and include:
•	
Intermittent renewable energy sources such as solar and wind, which are highly 
mature, with good global availability, a low levelized cost of energy (LCOE), and 
rapidly developing talent pools. The falling LCOE of these technologies means 
that in many cases they are the most viable option when adding new energy 
generation capacity, regardless of low-carbon goals.
•	
Dispatchable low-carbon energy sources, including renewable sources such as 
geothermal, hydropower, wave and tidal energy, plus nonrenewable low-carbon 
power sources such as nuclear fission and fusion.
Renewable energy is increasingly being used as a tool to improve energy 
independence for countries without their own conventional energy deposits, as 
renewable assets are not dependent on importing energy commodities. Energy 
storage is also growing in adoption, allowing easier integration of intermittent 
renewable energy sources into power networks—smoothing out some of their 
output variability—and also optimizing energy usage in buildings and facilities for 
commercial, industrial, and residential applications. Although we see VC-backed 
companies developing a broad range of technologies for energy storage, new energy 
storage capacity additions tend to involve lithium battery projects because of the 
maturity and relatively low cost of the technology.
Even incorporating the need for energy storage to balance the output of intermittent 
renewables, lower-carbon forms of energy generation can now be cost competitive 
with fossil fuel facilities. However, the commodity inputs—construction materials, 
base metals, and critical mineral resources—are different, exposing clean 
energy technologies to very different supply chain risks than their high-carbon 
counterparts. The speed of the clean energy transition has caused a rapid increase 
in demand for energy transition resources, and supply chains for these are often 
limited by geographically concentrated mineral deposits in addition to highly 
concentrated processing of these resources. Regionally concentrated mineral 
extraction and processing can result in supply chain vulnerabilities and bottlenecks 
with limited alternative sources if problems arise.
Global supply chain challenges may limit the speed at which countries can produce 
clean energy hardware, but further issues lie in the fact that the production of 
certain clean energy hardware is also highly geographically concentrated. In 
particular, the production of solar modules and lithium-ion batteries is highly 
concentrated in East Asia and Southeast Asia. Wider climate tech projects may also 
be at risk if the pace of clean energy adoption slows, as many of these technologies 
are dependent on clean energy to power them. Because these projects involve less

mature technologies, many are less able to pay the high premiums required for 
clean energy when compared with mature businesses in established sectors such as 
manufacturing and datacenter operation.
US tariffs
Recently, US President Donald Trump introduced a broad suite of global tariffs 
across a range of geographies and industries, seeking to boost domestic 
manufacturing and address perceived trade imbalances. Due to the breadth of the 
industries and regions covered, these tariffs have a strong potential impact on clean 
energy supply chains. These impacts are compounded by the strong uncertainty 
around how the tariffs may be changed. Recently, the US Court of International 
Trade challenged the sweeping tariffs that Trump introduced on “Liberation Day,” 
although the Trump administration has announced it will appeal this ruling.1
Since the Trump administration announced the initial set of tariffs, the details 
have changed considerably, with tariffs increasing and decreasing in magnitude. 
Exemptions have been put in place for certain sectors and regions while others have 
been particularly targeted. Although some tariffs have ultimately been enacted and 
will almost certainly continue to exist in some form, some of the initial waves of tariff 
announcements may have been used as a tool to encourage specific trade deals 
rather than policies that will remain at the stated magnitudes.
While tariffs affecting clean energy supply chains are not a new concept, the breadth 
of regions targeted makes alternative supply chains limited, and the magnitude of 
tariffs means that some sectors are not able to handle tariffs by reducing costs in 
other areas or passing on additional costs to customers. Ultimately, potential supply 
chain challenges—plus uncertainty around the future state of tariffs—are making VC 
investors more cautious to invest in certain clean energy technologies. Because of the 
ever-changing state of US tariff implementation, the effects on specific trade partners 
will have different impacts on global supply chains, further complicating the task of 
calculating the cost of tariffs and of finding the most suitable alternative suppliers 
of minerals and hardware. The uncertainty around tariffs is as much a factor as the 
tariffs themselves in many cases.
Industries and regions affected
Shared clean energy infrastructure
Individual clean energy industries are dependent on specific critical mineral needs, 
exposing them to unique supply chain risks and challenges. Most energy projects—
whether clean or conventional—also depend on a common set of material and 
component inputs, including basic materials for infrastructure projects, such as 
cement and steel, and components specific to certain power grids, such as copper 
and electrical hardware. While these materials and hardware components have 
long-established markets and supply chains, the US market in particular could see 
impacts due to recent tariffs, since the country imports significant percentages 
of cement, steel, and transformers from China, Canada, Mexico, and Europe. 
1: “Trump Tariffs Get to Stay in Place for Now. What Happens Next?” BBC News, Peter Hoskins and Yang Tian, May 30, 2025.

The US relies on Canada and Mexico as the two largest import sources for steel, 
while China and Germany are also in the top 10.2 Mexico and Canada together 
account for 27% of US cement imports;3 they also account for a significant share of 
imported electrical transformers.4 
Copper and steel supply chains can be bolstered to some extent through technologies 
such as recycling. Metal recycling is a fairly mature space, although $573.9 million 
in VC investment went to metal recycling technologies in 2024, marking a high point 
for the space. Further, VC investment in analytics for recycling and waste sortation 
can optimize recycling processes, improving the quality and quantity of materials 
that can be extracted from waste. From 2020 to 2024, there was an average of 
$263.5 million in annual VC deal value invested in recycling analytics technologies, 
mostly covering computer vision, machine learning, and robotics technologies for 
sorting waste more accurately.

Solar photovoltaics
Solar photovoltaic (PV) panels are a critical component of many regions’ energy 
plans, and the technology and manufacturing capabilities of the space are highly 
mature. When adding new energy generation capacity, solar is now one of the 
lowest-cost options,5 although manufacturing for the space is geographically 
concentrated in East Asia and Southeast Asia. Much of this manufacturing 
occurs outside the VC ecosystem, but we still see large deals from China-based 
manufacturers of solar hardware, including large deals in the last few years from 
Huakong Power, Huasun, and Astroenergy. Some of this regional concentration has 
been driven by China’s early investment in the manufacturing and production of 
solar components, but some is also driven by critical mineral extraction.

6: “China’s Export Controls Are Curbing Critical Mineral Shipments to the World,” Reuters, Lewis Jackson and Amy Lv, April 20, 2025.
7: “US Finalizes Tariffs on Southeast Asian Solar Imports,” Reuters, April 21, 2025.
8: “US Tariffs, Europe Slowdown Reshape Global Solar Panels Trade,” Reuters, Sudarshan Varadhan, May 8, 2025.
Although different solar PV panel types do not all rely on the same material 
inputs, some minerals are used in several of the most prevalent designs, including 
gallium, indium, and tellurium. Gallium extraction is highly concentrated in China, 
where it occurs as a supporting industry to aluminum mining. This dependency on 
aluminum mining makes scaling gallium extraction up or down more challenging, 
and it is also a headwind for other regions looking to develop their own gallium 
supply chains, as gallium extraction is most economical in regions with large 
aluminum extraction industries.
For regions outside China, this also makes solar PV hardware production highly 
dependent on importing specific minerals from China. This is even more challenging 
because China has placed export controls on certain critical minerals, including 
gallium—the export of which dropped 75.3% from March 2024 to March 2025.6
Tariffs are also a significant influence on the solar PV space. US tariffs for solar 
hardware are not a new phenomenon, and early tariffs on China-produced panels 
resulted in higher production in nearby countries Cambodia, Thailand, Vietnam, 
and Malaysia. Subsequently, US trade officials launched an investigation into solar 
hardware from these countries that concluded in 2024, although some additional 
investigations concluded in 2025. The investigations prompted the US to raise 
tariffs specifically on the solar industries of these four Southeast Asian countries. 
These countries face tariffs ranging from a 42% tariff on products from Chinese 
manufacturer JinkoSolar’s Malaysian operations to a 3,521% tariff on hardware 
from Cambodia, which was a penalty for not cooperating with the investigations.7 
In the short term, these tariffs have increased the US consumption of solar 
panels from manufacturers—owned mostly by Chinese companies—based in 
Laos and Indonesia.8

6
Tariffs and Supply Chain Challenges in Clean Energy
When adding new energy storage capacity, lithium-ion batteries remain one of the 
most widely deployed technologies due to their high energy density, falling costs, and 
mature manufacturing processes. While other technologies—such as flow batteries, 
sodium-ion batteries, and nonbattery energy storage—are seeing increased VC 
investor interest, lithium batteries currently dominate at the grid scale and among 
commercial, industrial, and residential deployments. This is partly due to the sector 
sharing a development ecosystem with the electric vehicle (EV) industry, which has 
resulted in rapid scaling and technological advancement. However, the performance 
requirements for stationary storage are very different from those of EVs. While EVs 
prioritize energy density and weight, stationary systems typically focus on cost, 
safety, and lifespan.
Lithium-ion batteries represent a broad category of battery technology, covering a 
range of chemistries with different performance characteristics and mineral inputs. 
Battery chemistries such as lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxides (NMC) are 
common in EVs due to their high energy density, but they are costly due to their 
reliance on the critical minerals nickel, cobalt, and manganese. Economically viable 
deposits of these materials are often concentrated in relatively small regions—cobalt, 
for instance, is heavily concentrated in Congo, although only about 5% of the mineral 
is mined by domestically owned mining companies.9 Much of the extraction is carried 
out by Chinese and European mining companies.
Graphite, used extensively for lithium-ion battery anodes, is another key input, 
and China dominates both natural and synthetic graphite processing. Some 
emerging technologies are exploring carbon-utilization pathways to produce 
synthetic graphite, potentially reducing dependence on mined sources. VC-backed 
companies in the space include CyanoCapture and CO2/Split, although this is a 
relatively small category within the carbon-utilization space, and most VC-backed 
companies tend to focus instead on the production of fuels, industrial chemicals, 
and construction materials.
For stationary energy storage, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) has now become the 
dominant battery chemistry. LFP batteries offer several advantages: They are less 
prone to thermal runaway, can have longer working lifespans, and do not require 
cobalt or nickel inputs, lowering their exposure to supply chain disruption risk.
Despite growing interest in domestic battery production in Europe and the 
Americas, Asia—particularly China—accounts for the vast majority of lithium 
battery manufacturing, which makes the sector highly sensitive to trade policy 
and supply chain disruptions. Attempts to build lithium battery production centers 
outside of Asia have met challenges. Northvolt, previously described as Europe’s 
answer to its reliance on nondomestic battery production,10 filed for Chapter 11 
protection in the US in 2024 and later filed for bankruptcy in Sweden in 2025, 
highlighting the challenges faced in trying to rapidly match the years of development 
enjoyed by China’s battery industry. US tariffs on Chinese products, in addition 
to China’s export controls on critical minerals, introduce challenges for clean 
energy supply chains. Producers of batteries based outside of China face problems 
9: “Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2024: Market Review,” International Energy Agency, May 2024.
10: “Northvolt Files for Bankruptcy in Sweden,” Northvolt, March 12, 2025.

when sourcing raw and processed critical minerals such as lithium, graphite, and 
manganese, and tariffs hinder clean energy adoption by hiking costs on hardware 
produced in Asia.
To combat the challenges of battery-material supply chains, VC-backed companies 
are developing technologies for both recycling end-of-life lithium batteries and 
for more efficient production of raw materials like lithium. The lithium battery 
recycling industry has become a critical component of the overall lithium battery 
space, and in some regions such as the EU, battery producers are required to 
manage their own recycling programs. Recycling processes focus on recovering a 
range of valuable materials such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, and copper. 
Extracting these minerals from end-of-life batteries can reduce the need for 
environmentally intensive mining while mitigating some supply chain challenges. 
VC-backed companies are developing advanced recycling technologies to improve 
recovery efficiency and reduce operational costs—mostly through lower energy 
input requirements. The largest VC-backed companies in the space include several 
North American companies, such as Redwood Materials, Ascend Elements, and 
Lithion, and the category saw $3.8 billion in VC deal value in 2023 before falling 
to $922.4 million in 2024.
VC-backed companies in the green mining space are developing a range of 
technologies to better extract lithium from brine and hard rock sources. Startups 
Lilac Solutions, Summit Nanotech, and ElectraLith are developing direct lithium 
extraction technologies. Lithium de France and Cornish Lithium are developing 
geothermal brine extraction technology, which couples heat and/or energy 
production from geothermal wells with the extraction of minerals from geothermal 
brine. Green mining processes have the additional benefit of reducing water 
consumption during the extraction process, which is typically very high.

8
Tariffs and Supply Chain Challenges in Clean Energy
The development of nonlithium battery chemistries has increased in recent years, 
largely driven by growing demand for energy storage and lower costs of production 
due to use of more abundant mineral resources. This includes flow batteries, 
metal-air batteries, and sodium-ion batteries, which are less reliant on rare mineral 
resources, although these technologies generally lack the energy density required 
for use in EVs and portable devices.
Metal-air batteries in particular, such as zinc-air and iron-air batteries, use widely 
available, low-cost mineral resources, simplifying supply chain management 
and reducing overall costs, although round-trip efficiency tends to be lower than 
most lithium-ion chemistries. Similarly, sodium-ion batteries rely on the far more 
abundant sodium rather than lithium, making them less vulnerable to supply chain 
disruptions, although, as with lithium-ion battery production, China continues 
to lead in sodium-ion battery production, with several major lithium-ion battery 
manufacturers investing in both chemistries.

Addressing clean energy supply chain challenges
The global clean energy transition faces significant risks due to the geographic 
concentration of supply chains for mineral resources and key hardware components 
such as wind turbine parts, solar modules, batteries, and electrolyzers. The 
production of these components is currently centered in Asia. This concentration 
represents a vulnerability—disruptions to any of these supply chains could

change has already added to tension between China and the US. While China 
dominates production of many strategic minerals, recent years have seen strong 
growth in global supply, helping to keep pace with rising demand. However, price 
volatility for certain critical minerals remains high, in some cases exceeding that of 
traditional energy commodities.11
While the most visible disruptions from global supply chain challenges are seen 
in solar PV and battery technologies, the broader clean energy sector is equally 
affected by systemic vulnerabilities. Tariffs, the geographic concentration of critical 
mineral extraction and refining, and heavy reliance on specific regions—particularly 
Asia—for hardware manufacturing have created bottlenecks in the clean energy 
industry. For US clean energy development, the geographic concentration of 
manufacturing, mineral extraction, and mining in regions such as Asia and Europe 
means that tariffs on these regions leave limited alternative sources for these 
products. This extends beyond clean energy generation technologies to impact all 
energy infrastructure projects, as grid modernization and transmission expansion 
currently depend on access to imported hardware and raw materials.
Scaling up mining and resource extraction outside of established regions such as 
China and Southeast Asia is challenging. Capital costs for scaling up extraction 
and refining operations in historically low-volume regions are significantly higher, 
creating headwinds for regions looking to improve their supply chain resilience. 
VC-backed companies are developing more efficient mining, resource extraction, 
and refining technologies to improve both upstream and downstream resilience.12 
Developments in subsurface resource detection from companies such as 
KoBold Metals and Ideon Technologies are improving exploration efficiency and 
reducing environmental impacts, while advances in supply chain management, 
warehousing, and freight logistics are helping to build more robust and adaptive 
supply networks.13 We also see some companies developing alternative processes 
for producing specific components of clean energy hardware, such as Niron 
Magnetics, which develops technology to produce permanent magnets that have 
key applications in the wind energy industry. Conventional permanent-magnet 
production supports the energy, automotive, and defense industries and relies 
on rare earth element extraction. China currently accounts for around 90% of 
global rare earth magnet production.14 These technologies—along with those for 
alternative energy storage and mineral extraction—offer ways to mitigate supply 
chain risks and continue clean energy adoption in regions that have so far relied on 
imported hardware and minerals.
